summary: The article traces summer fruits and vegetables from farm to table, drawing on interviews with a farmer, foreman, logistics expert, grocer, economist, tech CEO, chef and dietitian. It covers farming challenges, harvesting, the supply chain, local food miles, economics, agricultural technology, seasonal cooking and nutrition. It closes by stressing that consumers influence the market by buying local and seasonal.
one_line: A farm-to-fork look at summer produce, covering farming, supply chains, local markets, technology, cooking and nutrition, via interviews with industry figures.
key_facts: Rachel Nguyen, a third-generation farmer at Sycamore Acres, said summer is critical because 'Everything we've worked for comes to fruition.'
Nguyen said farmers must manage pests, drought and sustainable water usage while selecting crops.
Miguel Santos, Sycamore Acres' longtime foreman, said 'There's an art to harvesting' and that fruit must be picked at the right moment or it will go to waste.
Danny Vargas, a logistics expert with over a decade of experience in perishable goods transportation, gave a tour of a distribution center and said 'Time is of the essence.'
Refrigerated trucks carry produce to warehouses and distribution centers, and technology such as temperature controls and tracking systems mitigates spoilage risk.
Eliza Martinez, proprietor of Green Sprout Grocers, sources produce within a 50-mile radius and said 'Food miles matter.'
The author visited Green Sprout Grocers on September 18, 2023, and saw local tomatoes and peaches.
Agricultural economist Jamie Connors noted that summer 2023 saw a rise in certain input costs and increased consumer spending on premium produce.
At a September 22, 2023 demonstration at TechFarm Solutions, new machinery was unveiled that sorts and packs produce without bruising it, per CEO Arthur Kline.
Agriculture uses drone-assisted crop monitoring and collaborative robots (cobots) for picking to boost productivity and address labor shortages.
Chef Olivia Chen of Farmstead Table prepares a summer salad with heirloom tomatoes and sweet corn from neighboring farms, avoiding heavy sauces.
Dietitian Carlos Mejia said summer produce has high levels of vitamins, minerals and antioxidants and high water content that aids hydration.
Mejia suggested adding berries to breakfast porridge, slicing cucumbers for snacks and grilling zucchini for dinner.
